what_its_for: Rifapentine is an antibiotic used to treat or prevent tuberculosis (TB), a serious lung infection. It is almost always used together with other TB medicines as part of a combination treatment plan. Your doctor may prescribe it to treat active TB disease or to prevent TB infection from becoming active (latent TB).
how_to_take: Take rifapentine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass of water. You can take this medicine with or without food, but taking it with food (especially a meal containing some fat) may help your body absorb it better and can reduce stomach upset. Never skip doses or stop taking this medicine early, even if you feel better. Stopping too soon can allow the TB bacteria to come back stronger and harder to treat.
dosing: Your dose depends on what you are being treated for, your weight, and the other TB medicines you are taking. For active TB, it is commonly taken once or twice a week. For latent TB prevention, it is often taken once a week for 12 weeks along with another antibiotic called isoniazid. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Your pharmacist or doctor can confirm your exact dose and schedule.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose on your regular scheduled day. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist. Missing doses can make your treatment less effective, so try to take every dose as scheduled.
storage: Store rifapentine tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed. Store it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use any tablets that are past their expiration date.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase the risk of liver problems. Rifapentine can make many other medicines work less well, including birth control pills, blood thinners (like warfarin), HIV medicines, seizure medicines, and many others. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take. Women using hormonal birth control (pills, patches, rings, or implants) should use a backup method like condoms during treatment, because rifapentine can make hormonal contraceptives less effective.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (signs of liver problems), dark brown or tea-colored urine, severe stomach pain or vomiting, loss of appetite that does not go away, fever or chills, skin rash or itching, unusual bruising or bleeding, vision changes, or numbness or tingling in your hands or feet. Also call your doctor if you feel like your TB symptoms are getting worse or not improving. Note: This medicine can turn your urine, sweat, saliva, and tears orange-red. This is normal and not harmful, but it can permanently stain contact lenses and clothing.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few weeks, but it takes much longer for the medicine to fully kill the TB bacteria. It is very important to complete the entire course of treatment as prescribed, which may last several months. Do not stop taking your medicine just because you feel better. The full treatment is needed to cure TB and prevent it from coming back.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Rifapentine can harm an unborn baby. Your doctor will carefully weigh the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: This medicine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Safety and dosing in children varies by age and weight; your doctor will determine if this medicine is appropriate. Older adults: Older patients may need closer monitoring for side effects, especially liver problems. Liver or kidney disease: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney problems, as your doctor may need to adjust your treatment plan or monitor you more closely.
